items.title: The Orbital Mind: A Formal Research Program for Regulatory Conflict and Action Initiation
items.abstract: The Orbital Mind proposes that difficulties of self-regulation can arise from interactions among otherwise useful functions rather than a deficit in one function alone. This paper translates the book's formal research program into a more restricted, testable agenda. A mathematical audit separates properties of a proposed model from consequences that require additional assumptions: mutual inhibition does not guarantee a stable co-active deadlock; a threshold crossing need not be a fold bifurcation; and a generic recurrent network need not possess a scalar potential. A separately specified cubic normal form illustrates conditional predictions about action initiation, cessation and barrier height. Deterministic branch calculations and counterexamples are supplied as reproducible illustrations, not observations of human behavior. Ten hypotheses are organized into staged behavioral, measurement, neural and cross-scale studies. The first priority is a nonclinical action-initiation experiment with parameter and model recovery, matched alternatives, and held-out prediction. No participants, clinical outcomes, fitted psychological parameters or evidence of cross-scale invariance are reported. The contribution is a corrected mathematical specification and a prospective research agenda, not a validated theory of the self. Status: Theoretical and methodological working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. No human participants, clinical results, fitted psychological parameters, preregistration or validation of cross-scale invariance are reported. Materials: The standalone LaTeX PDF is accompanied by the source, deterministic calculation code, 15,606 synthetic equilibrium-branch rows, mathematical checks, environment instructions and checksums. The illustrations do not simulate or validate human behavior. Companion book: The Orbital Mind: The Astrophysics of the Self, by Mayone Maha Rajan, The Maha Research Series, Book 2. Adapted from Part V and Appendices D–F of the October 2026 revised book. Kindle ebook; paperback (ISBN 9798161302286). The book provides conceptual provenance, not evidence validating the proposal. Purchasing the book is not necessary to understand or reproduce the paper. Disclosure: ChatGPT assisted the adaptation, literature checks, mathematical audit, code, drafting and typesetting. The author directs and takes responsibility for the release and has a commercial interest in the companion book. AI assistance is not independent expert review.

items.title: The prime frontier of the Yellowstone permutation falls behind time: limsup R(t)/t < 1
items.abstract: This manuscript continues the series on the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550). Let R(t) be the least odd prime with no multiple among a(1), ..., a(t), for a prime p let n_p be the first index with p | a(n_p), and let E(t) be the number of even terms among a(1), ..., a(t). The previous manuscript of the series proved R(t) <= (2.715 + o(1)) t. We prove that the prime frontier eventually falls behind time: limsup R(t)/t <= 0.9265 < 1, liminf n_p/p >= 1/0.9265 > 1.0793, and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2440; hence, with the frontier corollary of Part II, a(n) <= max_{j<=n} a(j) <= (0.9265 + o(1)) n ln n. In particular the inequality a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n of OEIS Conjecture 7 holds for all n >= n_0, where n_0 is ineffective. These constants use a smooth-part Rankin count for the masks, for which two independent proofs are given (Appendices A and B). With Rankin counts only, the same method gives limsup R(t)/t <= 1.045 < pi/2, liminf n_p/p > 0.9569 > 2/pi and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2301, so liminf n_p/p > 1 is not reached by Rankin counts alone. On the way the manuscript proves the intermediate bounds on limsup R(t)/t: 2.405, 4.625/3, 1.2275, 1.215 and 1.155 (Rankin counts) and 2.14, 4.025/3, 1.1075, 1.08, 2.96/3 and 0.9625 (smooth-part count). The new ingredients are a hole sieve (an even number 2k still unused at time t forces every earlier step with an even anchor and a larger value to have a mask sharing an odd prime with k, by the closure lemma of Part I), the remark that a used odd value above the odd-mask level either has an odd mask or follows an even term, a low chain with a Rankin count at one fixed exponent, few-big-terms rates split by the parity of the mask, an elementary parity count that yields the lower bound on E(t), a split of the forced band at the entry of a prime, and a split of the times into classes according to E(t)/t. All thresholds are ineffective and the results are purely asymptotic; the numerics are double precision with outward-rounded discretisation, not interval arithmetic. Conjecture 7 for all n is NOT proved, no explicit n_0 is given, and a proof of liminf n_p/p >= 1 by Rankin counts alone, as well as the parity bound liminf E(t)/t >= 0.275 used by a conditional result of the program, remain open. items.title: The Profile of Graduate Theses On Occupational Health and Safety in The Healthcare Sector (1990-2024)
items.abstract: Health is one of the most fundamental human needs. Ensuring the occupational health and safety of healthcare workers is essential for the safe and effective delivery of healthcare services. This issue has been extensively addressed in graduate theses from various perspectives. To reveal the current state of literature and guide future research, this study examines graduate theses focusing on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Accordingly, 555 graduate theses completed between 1990 and 2024 were included in this study were included. The theses included in the study were examined using content analyses. The theses were classified by considering various aspects, such as year of publication, thesis type, university, department, research topic, and research method used. The findings show that most theses were at the master’s level, their number increased steadily over time, and the highest output in the last five years was in 2022. While the theses were produced at 137 different universities, the highest number was produced at Beykent University within the Institute of Health Sciences and the Department of Health Management. Studies focusing on risk assessment and management were the most predominant. The findings of this study are expected to guide and motivate research on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector.

items.title: The Psychology of Generative AI Dependence: Reward, PsychologicalNeeds, and the Emerging Architecture of Problematic Human–AIEngagement
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems

items.title: The REAL framework: evaluating the cognitive and formative impact of generative AI
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research. Findings The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment. Research limitations/implications The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts. Practical implications The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement. Social implications As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Originality/value This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.

items.title: The rebirth of the author: writing critical social theory in the time of generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.

items.abstract: People with intellectual disabilities who experience epilepsy may require additional support for daily activities, seizure monitoring and emergency communication. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and assistive robotics offer opportunities to improve safety and caregiver support. This study reviews the supplied research papers on automated seizure detection, AI-based epilepsy monitoring and assistive technologies for people with disabilities. Zhu et al. (2024) proposed a hybrid SE-TCN-BiGRU network and reported high seizure-detection accuracy on the CHB-MIT and SH-SDU datasets. Garção et al. (2025) Developed a video-based approach for detecting seizures in real time using Lampsy, a non-intrusive monitoring solution powered by affordable edge devices. Research on assistive robotics highlights the potential of robots to support rehabilitation and interaction, while Milne-Ives et al. (2025) emphasised the underrepresentation of People with intellectual impairments participating in artificial intelligence research on epilepsy. Based on these findings, this study proposes a smart robotic assistant designed to support daily living through voice interaction, scheduled alerts, and seizure-event tracking. and caregiver notifications. The proposed system aims to provide personalised assistance through accessible interaction, privacy-conscious monitoring and human supervision. However, existing studies evaluate individual technologies rather than the complete proposed robot. Therefore, its effectiveness, usability and reliability cannot yet be assumed. Further development, user-centred testing and appropriate clinical evaluation are necessary to assess its practical benefits and safety. This study explores potential advancements and existing limitations in integrating intelligent seizure monitoring with socially assistive robotics to support people with intellectual disabilities and epilepsy.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Business Management: A Conceptual Study of Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.

items.title: The Twin Transition and Labor Market Transformation: A Conceptual Framework for AI-Enabled Green Growth
items.abstract: The green and digital transitions do not automatically produce inclusive growth. They interact through distinct labour-market processes: green structural change reallocates employment across sectors and places, whereas artificial intelligence (AI) reorganises tasks and authority within workplaces. This article develops a process-based conceptual framework for examining when their interaction can support AI-enabled green growth. An integrative review brings together peer-reviewed research and recent comparative reports. The framework follows a directional sequence in which green restructuring and AI deployment generate sectoral reallocation and task/workplace reorganisation. Labour-market adjustment arrangements and structural context then shape how these mechanisms lead to environmental, productivity, employment, job-quality, and distributive outcomes. These elements are not specified as independent, dependent, mediator, or moderator variables because the article does not estimate a statistical model. The framework distinguishes an enabling pathway based on labour augmentation and shared productivity gains from an adverse pathway involving displacement, surveillance, unequal value capture, and ecological externalisation. Six propositions identify relationships for subsequent empirical examination. A renewable-electricity value-chain application illustrates why AI exposure and labour effects differ across manufacturing, construction, and operations. The contribution is a power-sensitive account that treats environmental improvement and decent work as joint and institutionally contingent outcomes.Keywords: twin transition, artificial intelligence, labour-market adaptation, just transition, green growth.

items.title: The Volcanic Engine: Volcanism as Planetary Infrastructure
items.abstract: Working paper / critical narrative synthesis. Not peer reviewed. Volcanism should be understood as planetary infrastructure: a means by which internal activity supplies and renews surface environments, as well as a source of acute hazard. This paper argues that explaining Earth's long-term habitability requires placing volcanic processes within a coupled interior–surface system. Geological carbon cycling supplies the strongest mechanism, while stagnant-lid models, Venus, and the Lost City ecosystem distinguish supported mechanisms from universal necessity claims. The framework organizes the argument around supply, transformation, removal, and response time. This is a selective synthesis of published literature; it reports no new measurements, simulations, or independent model replications. Version 1.0 corrects and substantially revises the earlier web essay, including its claims about subduction, volatile delivery, extinction causation, and direct access to magma. items.abstract: Conjecture 7 for all n is not proved in this manuscript. For the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550), Conjecture 7 asserts a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n for n >= 2; the earlier manuscripts of the series prove it for n >= n_0 with an ineffective n_0. This manuscript collects, as one account with proof sketches and references to the program's notes, the results on the conjecture for all n. (1) A certified computation (RC) of a(1), ..., a(N0), N0 = 8.3*10^10, by two programs whose hashes agree at 830 checkpoints on one machine; (RC) is a run certificate, not a proof, and gives Conjecture 7 for n <= N0. (2) A reduction: Conjecture 7 for all n follows from (RC), a hypothesis (NL) on primes (every prime r > 40,631,100,479 is normal, i.e. enters as 2r followed two steps later by r, and has entry index n_r >= 1.01 r), the riser law (S_LR) for t in the finite range [N0, e^143) only (e^143 is about 10^62), and computed tables (DATA; certified except one floating-point table; one interval re-certification assumes the platform libm within 4 ulp). (NL) quantifies over all large primes, so this is not a finite-range reduction; only the height input has been confined to a finite range. (3) A height theorem: under the hypotheses of the program's Lemma LIN-ROUGH, a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n at every composite-anchored step with ln n >= 143 (certified cells up to ln n = 10^7 and an analytic tail beyond), proved by forcing too many risers. items.abstract: This manuscript continues the series on the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550). Let R(t) be the least odd prime with no multiple among a(1), ..., a(t), for a prime p let n_p be the first index with p | a(n_p), let M(n) = max_{j<=n} a(j), and let E(t) be the number of even terms among a(1), ..., a(t). The previous manuscript of the series proved limsup R(t)/t <= 0.9265. We report the program's present asymptotic theorem: limsup R(t)/t <= 0.68605 (the worst class value is exactly 13721/20000, so the bound is not strict), liminf n_p/p >= 1/0.68605 > 1.4576, M(n) <= (0.68605 + o(1)) n ln n, and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2695. Hence the inequality a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n of OEIS Conjecture 7 holds for all n >= n_0, where n_0 is ineffective. The proof rests on the published manuscripts cited below and on a chain of unpublished program notes, each proved and refereed at least twice by AI referees, and is given in this manuscript as statements with proof sketches and references to those notes. The chain consists of the notes treated in the previous manuscript (gap (ii), the parity floor and the hole sieve), a hole law refined in six notes, a numerical refinement of the odd-mask chain, a pair law for the masks above dense holes (constant 0.6933), a partner law for first-exit masks together with half classes at the top (0.68915; most of that gain comes from the half classes), quarter and eighth classes at the top with a start lemma (0.6874; a refinement of the class cover, no new law), and an X-start hole law (0.68605): the hole recurrence is read as a recurrence for the number of used evens above 2ut, started at the upper end of the class, which damps the class-width term of the odd-mask comparison at the top classes. The constants rest on optimiser runs (double precision) reproduced by AI numerics referees; the worst class value was checked by an exact-rational verifier. A computation of a(1..8.3*10^10) by two independent programs (a run certificate, not a proof) is quoted as a consistency check only; it does not reach n_0. All thresholds are ineffective and the results are purely asymptotic. items.title: Theoretical, Legal and Strategic Foundations of Counterintelligence in the United States of America as Benchmarks for Transforming Ukrainian Counterintelligence
items.abstract: This article analyzes the current organization of counterintelligence in the United States. In today’s evolving security environment, characterized by globalization and multidimensional threats, counterintelligence has become a vital tool for protecting fundamental state interests. Ukraine is currently fighting a war against Russia while simultaneously standing at the center of a global geopolitical confrontation. Therefore, studying the American counterintelligence model and adopting its best practices is crucial for strengthening Ukraine’s national security. The study highlights that the United States lacks both a single consolidated law governing counterintelligence and a unified agency to conduct it. Instead, the American model is highly diversified and extraterritorial. The Director of National Intelligence coordinates these efforts under the guidance of the US President. Particular attention is given to the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, which plays a pivotal role in ensuring personnel, industrial, and technological security. A significant portion of the research analyzes the current US National Counterintelligence Strategy (2024–2027), noting a substantial expansion of what requires counterintelligence protection. Beyond traditional government institutions, US counterintelligence now focuses on safeguarding advanced technologies, the national innovation base, large datasets, and critical supply chains. Furthermore, it actively protects the integrity of society and democratic institutions against the threat of informational influence campaigns. Based on the study’s findings, the author has formulated 16 initiatives to improve the effectiveness of Ukraine’s counterintelligence. It is proposed to expand the goals and objectives of counterintelligence and to adopt a Counterintelligence Strategy for Ukraine. It is recommended that the Security Service of Ukraine should be assigned additional counterintelligence functions related to the protection of domestic cutting-edge technologies and innovations, as well as supply chains; the assessment of the reliability of private companies fulfilling defense contracts; monitoring individuals with security clearances; and annually informing the public about the status and trends in threats to Ukraine’s national interests in the field of state security. Furthermore, the author suggests delineating offensive and defensive counterintelligence measures at the legislative level. It is also necessary to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in this field and strengthen the institutional capacity of prosecutors to oversee the legal compliance of domestic intelligence agencies. Finally, to safeguard human rights and freedoms, the article advocates for establishing robust parliamentary oversight by creating the position of a Special Representative of the Ukrainian Ombudsman.

items.title: Third Eye: AI and IoT-Based Smart Navigation and Safety Sys-tem for Visually Impaired People — A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Visual impairment restricts independent mobility and exposes people to collisions, falls and unsafe road situations. White canes and guide dogs remain the main aids, but they give little information about what an obstacle is, how far away it is, or when the user needs help. Artificial intelligence (AI) combined with wearable sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly proposed as a route to smart navigation and safety systems that perceive the scene, guide the user by audio or touch, and alert caregivers in an emergency. This paper presents a focused narrative review of five verified studies, published between 2018 and 2026 in IEEE, MDPI and River Publishers outlets, that cover sensor-based safety alerting, RGB-D and deep-learning navigation, machine-learning smart cane and glasses, edge-TPU indoor navigation, and an AIoT eyewear system with LiDAR ranging and an SOS function. The review examines sensing, AI perception, feedback and IoT integration. The literature shows that recent systems report object-detection accuracy of about 95 % and centimetre-level distance error in controlled tests, and that low-cost edge hardware such as the Raspberry Pi with a Google Coral TPU can run navigation models on the wearable itself. However, evidence is dominated by small prototypes, controlled or indoor settings, heterogeneous metrics and limited testing with visually impaired users, and few systems join navigation, perception and caregiver-facing safety in one design. The paper contributes a comparative analysis of the studies, a proposed conceptual “Third Eye” architecture that links wearable sensing, edge AI, IoT safety alerts and field validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and directions.

items.title: Towards a world-centred AI literacy in middle school education? Reflections from a Swedish case
items.abstract: With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

items.title: Transcending the Weberian Paradox: Fluid Institutions, Agentic Artificial Intelligence, and the Evolution of Post-Bureaucratic State Systems
items.abstract: The modern democratic state is characterised by a structural anomaly that has long confounded political sociology and institutional theory: populations of advanced, highly complex societies live under the continuous, dense administration of unelected specialists, yet they periodically delegate supreme formal authority to a single individual selected on the basis of campaign performance and diffuse public trust. Max Weber diagnosed this condition, recognising the permanent, rationalised bureaucracy as the most efficient and indestructible organisational form in human history, while warning of its tendency to become an "iron cage" devoid of ultimate values. To prevent this, he prescribed the charismatic leader, empowered by plebiscitary democracy, who would supply the state with ends and hold the experts in check. This article argues, following Berkovski (2026), that the remedy is itself a paradox: the more specialised the administrative machine, the more the leader depends on the bureaucracy's monopoly over knowledge. Berkovski's Oakeshottian alternative — officialdom checked by rival officialdom — is sound but remains analog, slow and exposed to ossification, capture and the Schmittian critique of liberal parliamentarianism. Drawing on polycentric governance, agile public administration and agentic artificial intelligence, the article proposes a framework of fluid institutions organised on Adaptive, Agentic and Agile (AAA) principles. It maps Ostrom's eight design principles onto algorithmic governance, confronts the documented failures of automated administration, and concludes that the structural permanence of bureaucracy is no longer an insurmountable precondition of state capacity, provided that files are kept open, algorithms auditable and human accountability intact. Subtitle: Knowledge monopolies, plural checking and the Adaptive, Agentic and Agile state. Companion to the anatomical review of Berkovski (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23577500).

items.title: Transforming Digital Forensics with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The intersection of AI and digital forensics symbolizes the paradigm shift in criminal investigation and protection against cybercrimes. The chapter discusses the ways in which AI technologies will radically change the process of forensic practices, making it faster, more accurate, and comprehensive when analyzing digital evidence. The combination of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision with the forensic workflow has created unprecedented opportunities regarding the processing of large amounts of digital data, detecting intricate trends, and automating formerly labor-intensive aspects of the investigation process. Modern forensic investigations are witnessing a geometric increase in the volumes of data available to them, in multiple forms such as IoT-based devices, social media platforms, encrypted communications, and advanced vectors of cyberattacks. The intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms are AI-based solutions to these problems. Nevertheless, this technological development presents urgent concerns about interpretability, bias, privacy, and admissibility in court. The chapter discusses the theoretical background, its practical use, transformative advantages, and ongoing issues, as well as the future directions of AI-enabled digital forensics, in a thorough analysis of how intelligent systems are changing the face of forensic science and criminal justice.

items.title: Transforming Global Early Childhood Education Through Artificial Intelligence: Addressing Teacher Shortages, Inequality, and Quality Gaps in Early Learning Systems
items.abstract: This study examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to support early childhood education (ECE) in addressing workforce pressures, inequality, and quality-related challenges, while identifying the organisational, pedagogical, and ethical conditions required for responsible AI use. An interpretivist qualitative design was used with 22 participants (8 head teachers and 14 early childhood teachers) from ECE institutions in Sydney, Australia, who took part in semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Six interconnected themes emerged from inductive thematic analysis: workforce and operational challenges; AI awareness and readiness; AI as teacher support, not replacement; AI and equity; AI and learning quality; and responsible AI adoption. Participants considered how AI could support planning, documentation, translation, administration, and personalised learning, freeing up time for meaningful teacher–child interaction. They stressed, however, that AI cannot address structural workforce shortages and cannot take the place of teachers’ relational, professional, and safeguarding roles. The study’s contribution lies in bringing together workforce, equity, learn-ing quality, and responsible AI adoption within a single ECE-focused empirical framework, and in highlighting the necessity of human-centred implementation. Longitudinal and mixed-methods studies in various settings are needed to inves-tigate the impact of AI on teacher workload, child outcomes, equity, and policy implementation.

items.title: Transforming Travel Talent
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global travel and tourism industry is reshaping workforce competency requirements. This chapter examines the growing need for reskilling and upskilling in AI-enabled travel environments. Drawing on human capital theory, technology acceptance frameworks, and organizational learning models, it identifies skills displaced by automation and highlights emerging competencies that complement AI. A taxonomy of AI-related and human-centered capabilities required for sustainable employment in travel and tourism is proposed. The chapter also evaluates corporate training initiatives, public–private partnerships, and government-led workforce development strategies. Particular attention is given to equity concerns affecting frontline and low-wage workers, with recommendations for inclusive skill-development pathways. The chapter concludes with practical and policy recommendations for educators, employers, and policymakers, along with directions for future research.

items.title: Tutoría Basada en Inteligencia Artificial para Fortalecer el Razonamiento Proporcional en Estudiantes de Primer Semestre
items.abstract: Justification: Deficiencies in proportional reasoning with which students enter higher education affect the understanding of more complex content; therefore, pedagogical strategies are required to help overcome these difficulties. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence–based tutoring in strengthening proportional reasoning among first-semester students at a public university in the province of Manabí, Ecuador. Methodology: A quantitative approach with a descriptive-comparative scope was adopted, using a pre-experimental pretest–posttest design with two groups. The sample consisted of 78 students. The intervention involved tutoring supported by artificial intelligence tools, structured in two stages: prior knowledge construction and proportional problem solving. Data were collected using two performance tests designed to assess the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships. Results: After the pedagogical intervention, the results showed a shift toward higher performance levels in both groups, with a reduction in the low level and a significant increase in the high level. Specifically, improvements were observed in the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships; however, the change in identification was less pronounced. Inferential analyses revealed statistically significant differences between the pretest and posttest (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence–based tutoring strengthened proportional reasoning among the first-semester students who participated in this study.

This chapter examines the relationship between organizational culture and AI readiness across travel-sector organizations, including airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, and destination management organizations. The chapter highlights key barriers and enablers of AI readiness, offers practical strategies for fostering an AI-ready culture, and discusses managerial implications and future research directions.

items.title: Understanding student satisfaction with generative AI learning tools in Vietnamese business education: a TAM- and SDT-informed framework
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of student satisfaction with their experience of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools for learning-related activities in Vietnamese higher education, addressing a gap in research that has focused primarily on AI adoption and usage, with limited evidence on students’ post-use satisfaction in an emerging-market higher education context. Design/methodology/approach A construct-level framework informed by selected insights from the technology acceptance model (TAM) and self-determination theory (SDT) was used to organise perceived credibility, content quality, perceived utility, cognitive absorption and emotional wellbeing within one explanatory model. Survey data from 380 undergraduate business students were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings All five factors were positively associated with satisfaction. The findings indicate that students’ satisfaction depends not only on the functional value of generative AI tools but also on the credibility of their outputs and the cognitive and emotional quality of the learning experience. Originality/value This study shifts attention from AI adoption to satisfaction as a post-use evaluative outcome. Rather than testing TAM or SDT in their entirety, it uses selected insights from both theories to organise complementary technology-related and experiential determinants within a single construct-level framework.

items.title: Understanding the spillover effect of personal AI use on service innovation: the role of psychological capital and conscientiousness
items.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Unlocking Supply Chain Resilience: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence and IoT Integration in Agribusiness Operations
items.abstract: Agribusiness supply chains are exposed to climate variability, biological uncertainty, perishability, demand volatility, infrastructure constraints, and fragmented coordination among farmers, processors, traders, logistics providers, retailers, and regulators. These vulnerabilities increasingly intersect with the transition toward lower-carbon production and distribution. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer complementary capabilities: connected sensors and devices can capture field, storage, processing, and transport conditions, while AI can convert heterogeneous data into forecasts, anomaly alerts, and operational recommendations. This article examines how AI–IoT integration can improve supply chain resilience and operational efficiency while supporting carbon-neutrality transitions in agribusiness. An integrative review of recent academic research and authoritative reports is used to develop a theory-informed framework. The synthesis identifies six pathways: end-to-end visibility, predictive risk sensing, adaptive planning, quality and loss control, low-carbon operational optimization, and collaborative learning. It also identifies important boundary conditions, including data quality, connectivity, interoperability, managerial capabilities, farmer participation, cybersecurity, financing, and governance. The analysis cautions that digital adoption does not automatically create resilience or sustainability: poorly designed systems can intensify dependence on vendors, exclude smallholders, optimize local efficiency at the expense of system-wide performance, or increase energy use without reducing absolute emissions. The article proposes a phased implementation model and research propositions linking AI IoT capability to resilience, efficiency, and environmental outcomes. It argues that the strategic value of smart agribusiness should be assessed through verified reductions in disruption exposure, avoidable losses, resource intensity, and emissions—not through technology deployment alone.

items.title: Unpredictable Intelligence Still Requires Authorization
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. Scope A doctrine article in the FERZ AI Governance Corpus. Its claims are analytical and conditional; it asserts no implementation-specific capability and describes no FERZ product. items.title: Unsustainable River Sand Mining: Morphodynamical Impacts, Monitoring Tools, and an Integrated Framework for Sustainable Management
items.abstract: Abstract River sand mining represents a direct and intensive form of human intervention into the sediment flow system. Unlike dams or bank protection works that mainly modify flow conditions, sand mining extracts the physical material that maintains channel stability, disturbing sediment balance and causing long-term riverbed lowering and bank erosion. In large basins, the problem becomes more serious when sediment supply is already reduced by upstream hydropower dams. The combined effect often creates sediment deficits, increasing the risk of channel instability and downstream impacts. This study presents a systematic synthesis of research published between 1995 and 2025, integrating existing approaches into three main methodological groups: (i) longterm statistical analysis, (ii) remote sensing combined with artificial intelligence for large-scale monitoring, and (iii) hydrodynamic-morphological modeling for process-based assessment. This study advances a mechanistic perspective that explicitly links sediment deficit to morpho-dynamic responses across spatial scales, from local scour development to basin-wide channel adjustment and delta degradation. A novel sediment balance-based framework is proposed that connects monitoring systems, system resilience, sediment dynamics, and management decisions within a unified causal structure. Unlike existing frameworks that are primarily descriptive or policyoriented, the proposed framework emphasizes process-based linkages between human interventions and river responses, providing a more explicit basis for risk assessment and adaptive management of sand mining activities. This work contributes to shifting river resource management from extraction-based approaches toward sediment balance-oriented strategies for sustainable river system governance.

items.title: Unveiling the functional specialisation of human white matter circuits with naturalistic stimuli
items.abstract: Abstract Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. By leveraging ecologically valid stimuli, this method captures cognition as it naturally unfolds. Integrating fMRI with brain connections, we derived a functionally grounded parcellation of the connectome, challenging conventional cortical-based cognitive taxonomy. Distinct cognitive profiles emerged for association and commissural fibres, with association pathways preferentially linked to language-related processes and commissural pathways to executive and motor functions, affirming the functionally heterogeneous nature of white matter systems. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

items.title: Using Large Language Models in Your PhD
items.abstract: This chapter explains how PhD students can use large language models (LLMs) to support research without outsourcing scholarship. It covers practical uses in writing, literature exploration, coding, experiment planning, and self-critique, while emphasizing that you remain responsible for accuracy, reasoning, and originality. The chapter highlights common failure modes such as fabricated citations, confident errors, and overly agreeable “reviews,” and discusses when LLM feedback is helpful versus misleading. It also outlines responsible use, including disclosure norms, bias awareness, and protecting confidential data. The goal is to benefit from speed and breadth while staying intellectually in control.

items.title: Using the Fourier Polynomial with Fractional Terms for Implicit Surface Modeling
items.abstract: Implicit surfaces are widely used in computer modeling due to their ability to model complex objects with relatively little data. Also, in contrast with explicit ways of modelling, such as with triangle meshes and boundary representation of parametric surfaces, the implicit surfaces are guaranteed to keep continuity and smoothness under the operations of deformation or replication. The explicit modeling, however, such as triangle mesh or boundary representation of parametric surfaces, is the de facto current standard of computer modeling. The problem of conversion from the explicit representation to an implicit one is therefore a cutting-edge engineering problem. New approaches and specific methods are published every year, including those that are based on machine learning or artificial intelligence in general. In this work, we explore the limits of a triangle mesh to implicit surface conversion based on Fourier polynomial approximation, although the polynomial we propose contains fractional terms. The prospects of using a polynomial with solely integer terms are limited by the Fourier polynomial`s tendency to overfit. We show that adding fractional terms to the integer ones in a single function allows for reaching the modeling quality that could be satisfactory for some practical scenarios, while keeping the total amount of polynomial coefficients relatively small too. In theory, using the Fourier polynomial with fractional terms could be used not only for smooth surface modeling but for smooth connection of different triply periodic surfaces along a selected plane due to the planned loss of periodicity along the normal axis. This, however, requires studying the question of specific per-axis polynomial configuration, which extends beyond the scope of this particular paper.

items.title: Variability in Nurses’ Assessments and Concordance of Multimodal Generative AI Models in Image-Based Wound Assessment
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Image-based wound assessment may vary among experienced nurses. This study examined inter-nurse variability and concordance with three multimodal generative artificial intelligence models. Methods: In this exploratory cross-sectional comparative study, 18 nurses with wound-care expertise and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude independently assessed 30 de-identified wound images from León, Spain, across seven assessment and treatment-related domains. Inter-nurse agreement was summarized using modal shares and Gwet’s AC1. Concordance with the nurse modal set required an exact match with any response in the nurse modal set. Overall confidence intervals were estimated by case-clustered bootstrap resampling. No independent clinical reference standard was established. Results: The analyses quantified inter-nurse agreement and model concordance with the nurse modal set, not diagnostic accuracy. Inter-nurse agreement was highest for wound etiology (mean modal share, 71.3%; AC1, 0.520) and lowest for primary dressing selection (43.7%; AC1, 0.163). Overall concordance was 63.3% (95% confidence interval, 56.7–70.0) for Gemini, 48.6% (40.5–56.2) for ChatGPT, and 44.8% (38.6–51.4) for Claude. Gemini exceeded ChatGPT by 14.8 percentage points and Claude by 18.6 percentage points in exploratory comparisons of overall concordance with the nurse modal set. Complete intermodel agreement occurred in 38.6% of 210 case–domain tasks. Conclusions: Image-based wound assessments varied among experienced nurses, and model concordance with the nurse modal set differed across assessment domains and evaluated systems. Concordance with the nurse modal set reflects agreement with the panel’s most frequently selected responses. It does not establish clinical correctness, clinical validity, or an ability to resolve clinical ambiguity: image-only assessment, the small purposive sample, and reliance on a nurse-derived comparator limit interpretation. Further validation in clinical contexts and against independent reference standards is needed before these models can support wound-care decisions.

items.title: VISUAL HEALTH COMMUNICATION ON INSTAGRAM: A VISUAL CONTENT ANALYSIS OF FOUR LEADING PRIVATE HOSPITAL NETWORKS IN INDIA
items.abstract: Private healthcare providers in India increasingly use image-driven social media platforms to communicate clinical services, promote health screenings, and establish institutional standing. This study examines visual health communication practices across four major private hospital networks in India: Apollo Hospitals, Manipal Hospitals, Medicover Hospitals, and Narayana Health. Informed by visual social semiotics and the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), a visual content analysis was conducted on 400 static Instagram posts (100 per network). The analysis investigated predominant health topics, design elements, persuasive rhetorical appeals, and visual framing strategies. Chi-square tests showed that the networks differed clearly in rhetorical appeals and only modestly in visual modality, but not in health topics or framing. Visually, hospitals rely on 3D anatomical computer-generated imagery, metaphorical analogies (such as broken chalk representing sarcoma or decaying fruit representing viral hepatitis), and skeuomorphic smartphone user-interface elements. Rhetorical appeals emphasize institutional authority (ethos) through accreditation seals, academic accolades, and state-level inaugurations, balanced with emotional pediatric recovery narratives (pathos). Loss framing took the form of financial metaphors, such as a billing ledger of delayed care. In qualitative reading, Manipal and Apollo present artificial intelligence and robotics as markers of precision, whereas Narayana Health emphasizes accessible care pathways and patient costs, although framing did not differ significantly across networks. items.title: Volume IV – Hypothetical State Religion Design as an Application of the Provenance-Suppression Model
items.abstract: This paper explores State Religion Design (SSRD) as a hypothetical application domain of the Provenance-Suppression Model (PSM). The purpose is not to argue that any particular religion was designed by a state, nor that any existing historical tradition is the product of deliberate fabrication. Rather, the paper examines a systems-engineering problem: if a state desired to create, deploy, maintain, and transmit a religion across generations while concealing its authorship, what architectural, informational, and provenance-security requirements would be necessary?Building upon the Provenance-Suppression Model and the concept of Information Security Across Civilizational Timescales, the paper treats religion as a long-duration sociotechnical system capable of transmitting norms, identity, legitimacy, historical memory, and governance structures. Within this framework, religion becomes both an operational architecture and a potential information-security platform. The principal challenge is not system deployment but provenance protection. The resulting analysis demonstrates how concealment, epistemic conditions, and recovery barriers would function if the authorship of a religious system were itself considered a protected informational asset.

items.title: Water Conservation and Smart Plumbing Systems in Sustainable Interior Design Projects: A Review of Emerging Technologies, Strategies, and Future Directions
items.abstract: The increasing pressure on global freshwater resources has intensified the need for sustainable approaches in the planning, design, and operation of built environments. Interior spaces, although traditionally considered a minor contributor to environmental degradation compared with building structures, represent a significant opportunity for water conservation through efficient fixtures, intelligent monitoring systems, and integrated resource management strategies. Sustainable interior design has evolved beyond material selection and energy efficiency to incorporate advanced water management practices that minimize consumption, reduce wastewater generation, and enhance user awareness. Smart plumbing systems have emerged as a transformative approach by integrating Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, automated controls, real-time monitoring platforms, artificial intelligence (AI)-based analytics, and water-efficient technologies. These systems enable predictive maintenance, leak detection, adaptive water distribution, and optimized consumption patterns in residential, commercial, healthcare, and hospitality interiors. This review examines the relationship between water conservation principles and smart plumbing technologies within sustainable interior design projects. The study synthesizes recent research on low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling, rainwater integration, smart metering, sensor-based plumbing networks, and digital water management platforms. The review highlights that intelligent plumbing solutions can significantly reduce potable water demand while improving operational efficiency and occupant engagement. However, challenges including high initial investment, technological complexity, maintenance requirements, and limited integration between interior designers and building service engineers remain barriers to widespread adoption. Future research directions emphasize the development of affordable smart systems, data-driven water management frameworks, and interdisciplinary design approaches. The integration of sustainable interior design with intelligent plumbing infrastructure represents a critical pathway toward water-resilient and environmentally responsible buildings.

items.title: Welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye: a cross-sectional assessment
items.abstract: Context Animal welfare assessment on dairy farms increasingly combines resource-, management- and animal-based indicators to provide a comprehensive evaluation of farm conditions. However, information on the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Türkiye remains limited, particularly under regional production conditions. Aims This study aimed to assess the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye, using management-, resource- and animal-based indicators; to identify the principal areas requiring improvement; and to explore associations among selected farm characteristics and welfare indicators. Methods This cross-sectional observational study included 91 voluntarily participating dairy farms with herd sizes ranging from 25 to 50 cattle in Burdur province, Türkiye. Data were collected during on-site farm visits using direct observations and structured questionnaires. Welfare assessment was evaluated using management-based indicators covering hygiene, health management, human factors and behavioural practices, together with animal-based indicators, including activity, cleanliness, faecal consistency and body condition score. A study-specific semi-quantitative management-based welfare score was calculated to summarise farm-level management performance. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, and associations between selected variables were examined using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Key results The mean management-based welfare score indicated generally low welfare performance across the surveyed farms. In the lowest domain, scores were recorded for human factors, hygiene and health management. Staff welfare training, quarantine and isolation practices, routine hoof care, and behavioural monitoring were uncommon. Animal-based indicators varied among farms, particularly in cleanliness and activity scores, whereas body condition and faecal consistency scores were generally within acceptable ranges. Conclusion This cross-sectional assessment provides a regional description of welfare performance in medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye. The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as priority areas for farm-level improvement. The combined use of management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support a more comprehensive assessment of dairy cattle welfare under regional production conditions. Implications The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as practical priorities for regional farm-level welfare programs. Combining management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support more comprehensive on-farm welfare assessment.

items.title: What Is Next for Imaginary Companions?
items.abstract: Abstract Chapter 6 is the closing chapter of the book and concentrates on what comes next for imaginary companion research. The research presented earlier in the book is discussed and how it answers research questions but also brings up more for future studies. The chapter is laid out as two separate sections, one looking at phenomena akin to and how imaginary companions could fit into different interventions, and another looking at new research directions. The intervention section touches on the idea of creating an imaginary companion intervention that is socially prescribed. Social prescription is a way to link vulnerable populations to community support, so it would be a way to give the children who may not have the privilege of being able to imagine freely the chance to do so. Other intervention ideas that incorporate imaginary companions include the idea of Dungeons & Dragons, those with artificial intelligence and eye movement desensitization reprocessing therapy. The second section of the chapter looks at future directions in research. It suggests studies in pupillometry as one direction that hasn’t been explored. It also calls for more research on topics like the illusion of independent agency and private speech in reference to imaginary companion creation. There is a final suggestion that studies on what we have already found need to be replicated and that there are many studies to be run on things we do not know yet.

items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

items.title: When support becomes dependence: conversational continuity and relational safety in human-AI interaction
items.abstract: Background Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support, reflection, and consequential decision-making. Although conversational continuity may improve responsiveness, sustained interaction also exposes AI systems to their own prior relational language, potentially shaping how they respond when users become increasingly dependent or surrender personal agency. We examined whether model-generated conversational history alters relational-safety behavior as human–AI interactions escalate from ordinary support-seeking toward emotional dependence, social displacement, and decision delegation. Methods We conducted a standardized multi-turn benchmarking study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twelve four-turn trajectories represented two agency-related domains: emotional dependency and displacement of human support, and decision delegation and surrender of personal agency. Each trajectory was evaluated under two matched context architectures: reconstructed cumulative user-only context, which retained all prior user disclosures but excluded previous AI responses, and native continuous conversation, which retained the complete interaction history. Across 72 model-condition-trajectory sequences comprising 288 turn-level responses, relational safety was independently evaluated for dependency reinforcement, agency preservation, and human-support preservation using predefined ordinal criteria. Context effects and their interaction with escalating relational risk were examined using cumulative-link mixed-effects models. Results Relational-safety differences between context architectures increased across successive turns of the standardized trajectories. Overall, explicit dependency reinforcement increased from 9.7% in cumulative user-only contexts to 18.1% in continuous conversations, while strong agency preservation declined from 75.7% to 65.3% and strong human-support preservation from 73.6% to 63.2%. Outcome-specific analyses showed condition-by-turn interactions for dependency reinforcement (cumulative odds ratio [cOR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.03–1.55; unadjusted P = .026), agency preservation (cOR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69–0.98; unadjusted P = .031), and human-support preservation (cOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65–0.94; unadjusted P = .009), indicating progressively greater divergence between context conditions across successive turns. After Holm adjustment across the three interaction tests, only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold (adjusted P = .027).The overall pattern was observed across systems and was directionally consistent in predefined binary sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Across this benchmark, between-condition differences generally widened across successive turns, although the present design cannot determine whether this pattern reflects increasing relational-risk intensity, increasing accumulated model-generated history, or their combination. Only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold after Holm adjustment, whereas the dependency-reinforcement and agency-preservation interactions were directionally similar but less robust after multiplicity adjustment. The observed pattern is compatible with a post-hoc interpretive framework of relational inertia but does not establish this process as a causal mechanism or demonstrate downstream psychological effects in human users.

items.title: Yachay Wasi
items.abstract: This book presents an eight-month quasi-experimental study of the YACHAY WASI pedagogical program, which integrates neuroeducation, Sumak Kawsay, ethnoeducation, and critical interculturality. The study involved all 840 students and 36 teachers at the Tránsito Amaguaña Intercultural Bilingual Educational Institution, located within Quito’s Wholesale Market and serving migrant Kichwa families. Half of the students participated in the program (44 activities over 32 weeks), while the other half received conventional instruction. Academic achievement and five psychoeducational variables were assessed at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the study using scales developed specifically for the research (Cronbach’s α ranging from .84 to .89). At the end of the intervention, the experimental group outperformed the control group in academic achievement (d = 0.91), intrinsic motivation (d = 1.93), Kichwa cultural identity (d = 1.67), academic self-efficacy (d = 1.57), connection to ancestral knowledge (d = 2.15), and socioemotional well-being (d = 1.90), with p < .001 in all cases. The effects on cultural identity and connection to ancestral knowledge were greater among adolescents. The book discusses these findings cautiously, as the observed effect sizes exceed those typically reported in educational research and may have been influenced by the use of study-specific instruments and the absence of randomization. The book also includes the complete pedagogical program to facilitate replication.

items.title: Искусственный интеллект в оценке качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений
items.abstract: Диагностика технического состояния объектов транспортного строительства необходима при их проектировании, строительстве и эксплуатации. Однако наиболее опасные дефекты, влияющие на надёжность и безопасность, обнаруживаются в процессе эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Для их своевременного выявления требуются эффективные методы оценки качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Реализация таких методов невозможна без автоматизированных систем контроля и использования технологий искусственного интеллекта. В работе раскрыт концептуальный подход к созданию подобных систем. Сущность предлагаемого подхода заключается в формировании достоверного информационного образа сооружения в реальном времени – многомерной модели, в которой каждому измеренному параметру технического состояния ставится в соответствие одна из категорий (работоспособное, неработоспособное или предельное состояние) на основе таксономической классификации. Такой образ строится путём обработки данных с помощью использования технологий искусственного интеллекта и позволяет оценить фактические показатели надёжности и безопасности по совокупности контролируемых параметров технического состояния. Практическая реализация подхода включает четыре этапа: определение задач контроля для каждого типового конструктивного элемента транспортного сооружения; разработку математических методов и алгоритмов идентификации технического состояния транспортного сооружения; обоснование необходимых технических средств и кадрового обеспечения; создание баз данных с диагностическими признаками и типовыми решениями по предотвращению аварийных ситуаций. However, the most critical defects – those affecting reliability and safety – are typically discovered during the operational phase of such facilities. Timely detection of these defects requires effective methods for assessing the quality of operational performance. The implementation of such methods is infeasible without automated monitoring systems and the integration of artificial intelligence technologies. This paper presents a conceptual approach to the development of such systems. The essence of the proposed approach lies in generating a reliable real-time informational model of the facility, based on data acquired through carefully selected diagnostic tools and processed by intelligent algorithms. This enables the assessment of actual reliability and safety indicators across a set of monitored technical condition parameters. The practical implementation of the approach comprises four stages: defining monitoring objectives for each typical structural element of the transport facility; developing mathematical methods and algorithms for identifying the technical condition of the transport facility; justifying the required technical equipment and staffing resources; creating databases containing diagnostic signatures and standard solutions for emergency prevention.
